transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: The world's largest wind farm has officially opened off the coast of Denmark, capable of producing enough electricity to power over one million homes. The project, which took four years to complete, consists of 165 massive wind turbines spread across an area of more than 150 square kilometers in the North Sea. Each turbine stands over 200 meters tall, with blades longer than a football field. Danish officials say the wind farm is a major milestone in the country's ambition to become carbon neutral by 2050. The project has also created thousands of jobs in manufacturing, construction, and maintenance. Energy analysts predict that offshore wind energy will play an increasingly important role in Europe's energy mix in the coming decades, as countries move away from fossil fuels to combat climate change. However, the project has not been without criticism—some environmental groups have raised concerns about the impact of wind farms on marine life and bird populations, though the Danish government says extensive environmental studies were conducted before construction began.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: A new report from the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization indicates that global food prices have reached their highest level in a decade. The FAO's Food Price Index, which tracks monthly changes in the international prices of commonly traded food commodities, rose for the fifth consecutive month in July. The increase has been driven primarily by rising prices for vegetable oils, sugar, and cereals. Economists attribute the price hikes to several factors, including extreme weather events affecting crop production in major exporting countries, supply chain disruptions caused by the pandemic, and increased demand for biofuels. The report warns that high food prices could have serious consequences for low-income countries that are heavily dependent on food imports, potentially leading to increased food insecurity and social unrest. The FAO is urging governments to monitor food markets carefully and take measures to protect vulnerable populations from price volatility.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: A Japanese technology company has developed a new type of robotic suit that can help elderly people and those with mobility issues walk more easily. The device, which weighs only about three kilograms, is worn around the user's waist and legs. It uses sensors and small motors to detect the wearer's movements and provide additional support to the leg muscles when walking or climbing stairs. In clinical trials involving over 200 participants, users reported a significant reduction in muscle fatigue and a noticeable improvement in stability when using the suit. The company says the device is designed to be comfortable to wear for extended periods and can be adjusted to fit different body types. They plan to begin selling the robotic suit to hospitals and nursing homes next year, with a consumer version becoming available within the next three years. The technology is expected to be particularly useful in Japan, where nearly 30 percent of the population is over 65 years old, and demand for elderly care assistance is growing rapidly.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Noah): Hey, Mia. How's your part-time job at the campus bookstore going? I was thinking about applying there myself.

Woman (Mia): Oh, it's not bad at all, actually. The pay is decent for campus work, and the staff are really friendly. But you should know that it can get pretty busy during the first few weeks of the semester when everyone's buying textbooks.
Man: That makes sense. What are your hours like? Do they work around your class schedule?

Woman: Yeah, they're really good about that. All the employees are students, so they understand that classes come first. You just tell them your available times each week, and they schedule you accordingly. I usually work three evenings a week and Saturday mornings. It works out to about 15 hours a week, which is manageable with my course load.
Man: That sounds ideal. I don't want to work more than that, because I'm taking 18 credits this semester. What do you usually do there—just work the cash register?

Woman: There's a lot more to it than that. When I first started, I was mostly restocking shelves and helping people find their textbooks. Now that I've been there for a while, I also help with processing online orders and doing inventory once a month. Sometimes I help professors order books for their courses too. It's actually pretty interesting—you get to know what books are being used in all kinds of classes.
Man: Is there anything I should know before applying? Like, do they require any previous experience?

Woman: No, not really. They train you on everything you need to know when you start. But I will say that it helps if you're comfortable talking to people, because you get asked a lot of questions. Also, the busiest times are the first two weeks and then again during finals week when people are selling their books back. But there are also slow periods where there's not much to do, and you can get some studying done when it's quiet.
Man: That sounds like a perfect setup. I'm going to stop by tomorrow and pick up an application. Do I need to submit a resume or anything?

Woman: Just fill out the application form they give you, and they'll probably ask for a copy of your class schedule too. I'm pretty sure they're hiring right now because they always need extra people for the textbook rush. Good luck—I hope we end up working together!

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Logan): Ava, did you see that announcement about the campus film festival that's happening next month? I was thinking about entering.
Woman (Ava): Really? I didn't even know about that. What kind of films are they looking for?

Man: Any kind of short film, really—fiction, documentary, animation, experimental. They just have to be under 15 minutes long, and you have to be a current student. The winner gets a $500 prize, and their film gets shown at the campus theater, plus they get to meet some professional filmmakers who are coming to judge.

Man: I've made a couple of short films for classes, and I have a decent camera and editing software on my computer. But I can't do it all alone—I was wondering if you'd want to work on it with me? I know you're really good at writing stories, and I could really use someone to help with the script and maybe do some of the filming too.
Woman: I'd love to! That sounds like so much fun. But what would the film be about? We only have a month to make it, so we need something we can actually do without a big budget or anything.

Man: I was thinking about doing a documentary about the different food trucks on campus. Everyone loves the food trucks, but I don't think most people know the stories behind them—you know, who owns them, how they got started, what their most popular dishes are. We could interview the owners, film them cooking, talk to students who eat there. It would be fairly simple to shoot, and it's a subject that everyone can relate to.
Woman: Oh, that's a great idea! I love the Thai food truck by the library—their pad thai is incredible. I'd love to meet the people who run it. How much time do you think we'd need to spend on this?

Man: If we started this weekend, we could probably do most of the interviews in the first two weeks, then spend the third week editing. We'd need to borrow some microphones from the media department, but they let students check out equipment for free. I already have a good microphone I can use too.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The history of coffee is a fascinating journey that spans centuries and continents. While coffee is now one of the most popular beverages in the world, consumed by billions of people every day, its exact origins are shrouded in legend. The most famous story involves an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi who noticed that his goats became unusually energetic after eating berries from a certain tree. When he tried the berries himself, he experienced a similar burst of energy. He brought the berries to a local monastery, where the monks initially dismissed them as the work of the devil and threw them into the fire. However, the aroma from the roasting beans was so enticing that they decided to make a drink from them, and they found that it helped them stay awake during long hours of prayer.

From Ethiopia, coffee spread to the Arabian Peninsula, where it was first cultivated on a large scale in Yemen by the 15th century. Coffee houses, known as "qahveh khaneh," quickly became centers of social and intellectual life in cities across the Middle East. People would gather there to listen to music, play chess, discuss politics and news, and of course drink coffee. These establishments became so important as centers of information exchange that they were often referred to as "schools of the wise."

Coffee arrived in Europe in the 17th century and initially faced suspicion and controversy. Some people called it the "bitter invention of Satan," and in Venice, local clergymen even condemned it. However, when Pope Clement VIII tried coffee himself, he was so impressed that he gave it his approval, declaring it a Christian beverage. Coffee houses soon spread across Europe, becoming important meeting places for businessmen, philosophers, artists, and writers. Lloyd's of London, the famous insurance exchange, actually started as a coffee house in the late 1600s.

Coffee came to the Americas in the 18th century, when a French naval officer named Gabriel de Clieu brought a coffee plant to the Caribbean island of Martinique. From that single plant, much of the world's coffee supply would eventually grow, as coffee cultivation spread throughout South and Central America. Today, coffee is grown in over 50 countries around the world, mostly in equatorial regions, and it remains one of the most valuable traded commodities globally.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: Procrastination, the habit of delaying important tasks until the last minute, is something that almost everyone has experienced at some point. But while many people think of procrastination as simply being lazy or having poor time management skills, psychologists have found that it's actually a much more complex issue related to our emotions and how we cope with stress.

Research shows that people often procrastinate not because they lack willpower, but because they're trying to avoid negative emotions associated with a task. For example, if you're anxious about writing a paper because you're afraid it won't be good enough, or if you're feeling overwhelmed by a big project, putting it off temporarily makes you feel better by avoiding that anxiety. The problem is that this relief is only temporary, and the stress comes back even stronger as the deadline approaches. This creates a cycle where procrastination leads to more stress, which leads to more procrastination.

Interestingly, studies have found that procrastinators actually create unnecessary stress for themselves. In one experiment, college students who were given a deadline for a paper were divided into two groups: those who said they would finish early and those who admitted they would procrastinate. The procrastinators not only turned their papers in later, but they also reported more stress and illness throughout the semester, and they received lower grades on their papers.

So how can people overcome procrastination? One effective strategy is to break large, intimidating tasks into smaller, more manageable steps. Instead of thinking "I need to write a 20-page paper," think "I'll just write the introduction today, that's only a page or two." This makes the task feel less overwhelming. Another helpful technique is the "two-minute rule"—if a task takes less than two minutes to complete, do it right away instead of putting it off. For larger tasks, committing to just five minutes of work can help you get started, and often once you've begun, you'll find that you want to keep going. Finally, being kind to yourself when you do procrastinate instead of being harshly self-critical actually makes it less likely that you'll procrastinate again in the future.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Urban beekeeping has been growing in popularity in cities around the world over the past decade, as more people become aware of the important role bees play in our food system and the environment. While many people might think that bees only belong in rural areas, cities can actually be excellent habitats for honeybees, often better than some agricultural areas that use large amounts of pesticides.

One reason bees thrive in cities is that urban gardens, parks, and even balconies and window boxes provide a diverse range of flowering plants that bloom throughout the growing season. Unlike large farms that might only grow one type of crop, cities offer a variety of trees, flowers, and shrubs that give bees a consistent food supply from early spring through late fall. Many cities also have fewer pesticide problems than intensive agricultural areas, making them safer for bees.

The benefits of urban beekeeping extend beyond just helping bee populations. Bees are essential pollinators, and having hives in the city can help increase yields for community gardens and urban farms, as well as supporting the growth of native plants. Local honey produced by urban bees is also becoming popular—many people believe that eating small amounts of local honey can help with seasonal allergies, though scientific evidence for this is mixed. Additionally, beekeeping can be an educational and therapeutic hobby, bringing communities together and helping people feel more connected to nature even in the middle of a big city.

Of course, urban beekeeping isn't without its challenges. City ordinances sometimes restrict or prohibit beekeeping, though many places are updating their regulations to be more bee-friendly. Beekeepers also need to be responsible about managing their hives to make sure they don't become a nuisance to neighbors. This includes providing adequate water sources so bees don't end up in swimming pools, placing hives in appropriate locations, and being prepared to manage swarming behavior.

Despite these challenges, the urban beekeeping movement continues to grow. Major cities like Paris, London, New York, and Tokyo have all seen huge increases in the number of registered beehives over the past decade. Many cities now offer beekeeping classes, and some hotels and office buildings even keep hives on their rooftops. It seems that even in our modern, concrete-filled cities, people are recognizing the value of making space for these important insects.
